# Dream Control as a Diagnostic

## The Question You Ask Yourself Before Sleeping

There's an instruction in the Tantric material on the clear light that turns the whole dream business inside out.

> As instructed before in the Dream Yoga, one should observe whether he is confident and able to master the Bardo. He should ask himself, "With my present Realization can I master the Light-of-Death when the time comes?" If he can master the Four Voids of Sleep, he can be assured of recognizing the Four Voids at the time of death.[^1]

Dream control isn't the goal. It's the test.

What you actually need to be able to do is stay awake through the dissolution at death and recognise the light when it comes. That happens once. You can't practise it, and nobody who has done it can tell you how it went. So the tradition reaches for a substitute: the same sequence, at no stakes, available every night, free.

The four voids of sleep and the four voids of death are claimed to be the same four, which is what makes the substitution work at all. Master the first set and you're *assured* of recognising the second. That's the transfer claim, and everything else here hangs off it.

And the light itself isn't something the practice makes. *The Light-of-Origin, or of Reality, is the Innate Light that exists at all times regardless of whether one is aware of it or not.*[^1] It's there tonight whether you catch it or not. The practice only changes whether you're there when it happens.

## Hold Your Breath and Let It Out Slowly

The Tibetan instructions for this are described as complicated — *you must bring your chi to rest in your throat chakra so that you can cultivate this form of exercise* — and then set aside for something you could do tonight.

> However, all you really have to do is hold your breath and then release it slowly in such a way that your chi comes up to your head. If your chi comes to your head, you're likely to have lucid dreams that night, or dreams that you're flying.[^3]

Chi is the body's moving energy, the thing that goes where your attention and your breath send it. Hold the breath, then let it out slowly and in a way that draws that energy upward into the head. That's the entire instruction. No chakra to locate, nothing to visualise, no sequence to memorise.

And it comes with a marker that arrives the same night. Lucid dreams, or dreams of flying. If neither shows up, the chi didn't go to the head, and you know within about eight hours rather than within a decade.

The reasoning is stated outright: *that's actually the scientific principle behind this practice, which is to bring the chi to the head and try to remain cognizant during your dreams.*[^3] Two moves, in that order. Get the energy up there. Then try to stay awake inside the dream and see through it to what's underneath.

There's also a window. The clear light of sleep *occurs just before waking or falling asleep*[^3] — not in the middle of the night and not during the dream proper, but at the two edges. Which is why the Kashmir Shaivite line quoted alongside it is an instruction rather than a poem: *if you maintain your awareness at that point which is found between waking and sleeping, you will be focused on that supreme felicity which is the supreme bliss of God Consciousness.*[^3] The target is a boundary, not a place.

## Two Things That Must Be True First

Before any of that, there's a gate, and it's raised as a complaint that the schools teaching this leave it out.

> before someone even considers whether they are qualified to practice the methods of dream yoga, this school neglects to stipulate that practitioners must first be sure that their chi mai are in really good condition, particularly the chi mai of the stomach and intestines.[^3]

The *mai* are the channels the body's energy runs in. So the first condition is physical and unglamorous: the gut has to be in good order. Given that the same pages file the ghost sitting on your chest under overeating, the gut is where dreams are being made anyway.

The second condition is about temperament, and it's the one that will disqualify the people most drawn to this:

> potential practitioners should not be "dreamy," absentminded or "spacey" individuals to begin with because this type of practice may even exacerbate their problem.[^3]

Not *it won't work for them*. It'll make them worse. The people who most want to spend their nights inside their own heads are the ones told to stay out.

And the risk if you go ahead anyway is named plainly: *if a person goes the wrong way when involved in these types of practice, they can easily become mentally unbalanced and can even go crazy.*[^3] Underneath all three warnings is what's being worked with. The *du-yin* — the consciousness that runs during dreams — also runs during insanity, during incoherence, and during certain states of meditation. Instinct, inspiration and what people call a sixth sense all belong to it. Artists, religious people and writers are said to have more of it active than most.[^3] So the faculty this practice trains and the faculty that comes apart in mental illness are being described as the same faculty, which is why the conditions are conditions rather than suggestions.

## Water Into Fire, Then the Street Outside

The practice proper has three stages, and only the first one is what people mean by lucid dreaming. At the start you take on simple tasks — *trying to transform water to fire in their dreams.*[^3] Change one thing into another and see that it changes. That's stage one, and it's where the commercial courses stop. The stated purpose runs past it: *the purpose in dream yoga is not just to gain control of dreams but to cultivate a certain wakefulness and ultimately a glimpse into the ultimate mind essence.*[^3]

Stage two moves out of the bed. *While you're awake you start upon the practice road of experientially realizing that everything is like a dream.*[^3] Not thinking it. Realising it while the bus is late and the shopping is heavy — the same recognition you had at three in the morning, carried into the afternoon.

Stage three closes the loop: *you learn how to actually change things in the waking state just as you could during your dreams*, and it comes with the changes in mental state, chi and channels that go with that realisation.[^3] Then the reasoning behind stage three, which is worth having even if you never get near it. *This transformative ability is actually close to a sort of prajna wisdom because with prajna, you can visualize something and it will manifest. Why is that possible? Because no scenario is real; they all change according to our mind.*[^3] Prajñā is the wisdom that sees things as they actually are; the claim is that if nothing was ever fixed, changing it isn't a violation of anything.

And then the ceiling, stated against the tradition being described: *the dream yogas of the Esoteric school never really reach this sort of level.*[^3] Three stages are laid out and the third is said not to be arrived at by this route. Which puts a limit on the whole practice from inside the passage that teaches it.

## Mirage, Smoke, Fireflies, Light

The rehearsal only makes sense if sleep and death run the same sequence, and the death side gets set out in detail.

> First, when the element of earth dissolves into water, the nāḍī-knot at the navel disintegrates… the body feels heavy, consciousness fades, and an experience that is like a mirage appears.
> Next, when water dissolves into fire, the nāḍī-knot at the heart disintegrates… the mouth and nose dry out, consciousness is restless, and an experience resembling smoke arises.
> Third, when fire dissolves into wind, the nāḍī-knot at the throat disintegrates… body temperature grows faint, perception vacillates, and an experience that is like fireflies arises.
> Fourth, when wind dissolves into consciousness, the nāḍī-knot at the secret place disintegrates… the breath stops moving through the nostrils… and a slight appearance of light appears.[^2]

Four dissolutions, four knots, four signs. A mirage. Then smoke. Then fireflies. Then a faint light. Each one is tied to a physical event you could watch from the bedside — the body going heavy, the mouth drying, the warmth leaving, the breath stopping.

The bridge to the living version is that the same appearances turn up in practice: *an advanced cultivation practitioner will experience many visaya that are similar to the same visaya experienced when the chi starts entering the sushumna central channel.*[^2] The *sushumna* is the central channel up the spine, and *visaya* here just means what shows up in experience. So dying and the energy entering that channel produce the same class of appearance, and if falling asleep runs a shortened version of it, holding awareness through it is one skill practised in two places.

What makes it worth doing every night is what's said to be waiting at the end: *death is just your sixth consciousness moving to a new place, and there is a moment in the process when the sixth consciousness collapses so that you can see the Tao.*[^2] The sixth consciousness is the part of you that sorts and labels everything. The threshold this whole tradition is organised around is its collapse — and that happens to everyone, once, at the end, without any practice at all.

The catch is obvious once it's said. The collapse takes the labelling faculty away, and the labelling faculty is what would have noticed. So the opportunity is universal and being able to use it isn't, and a nightly rehearsal is exactly the right response to that.

## The Ghost on Your Chest Is Your Dinner

Alongside all this sits a classification of dreams by what causes them, and the first two rows are the useful ones. Dreams of sickness and health come first. Eat too much, get indigestion overnight, and *you might dream of a ghost or heavy object resting on your body.* Get too hot and *you might dream of an oven or fire.*[^4] A tradition that files the pressing weight on your chest under supper rather than under visitation is doing the same thing as the practitioner who reached for the meditation belt before reaching for a demon.

Then dreams from ordinary thought mixed with deep desire. Somebody who wants to get rich dreams of the stock market; at the far end of the same category, somebody sleepwalks.[^4]

The remaining rows — outside influence from spiritual beings, clairvoyant dreams, and dreams of past lives reaching *the seeds in the alaya storehouse consciousness* — carry material excluded from this vault and handled on the companion page. 🚩 Nothing here rests on them.[^4]

The point of the classification is that it's diagnostic before it's anything else. Before you ask what a dream means, you ask what made it. And most of the time what made it was dinner, or the thing you spent all day wanting.

## Implementation Workflow

Start with the gate, because it's the part that gets skipped. How's your digestion? If your stomach and intestines are in poor order, this isn't the practice to be doing, and the reason is that the material dreams are made of is coming from there. And be honest about the second question, which is harder: are you already a bit dreamy, absent, prone to drifting? If somebody who knows you well would say yes, the instruction is to leave this alone, because it makes that worse rather than better.

If both are clear, tonight's version is one breath. Lying down, hold your breath, then let it out slowly, drawing the energy up towards your head as it goes. Then wait and see what turns up. If you dream you're flying, or you notice mid-dream that you're dreaming, the chi went where you sent it. If nothing does, it didn't, and you try again tomorrow. It's the rare instruction in this book that reports back inside a day.

Then use it as the test rather than as the trophy. Not *was the dream vivid* and not *could I change things in it* — those are stage one, and stage one is what the courses sell. The question is whether anyone was home across the boundary. Falling asleep, and again on waking: did awareness go out like a light, or did something stay on through the changeover? That's the only reading that matters, and it's the reading the readiness question asks for.

Then ask the readiness question itself, in the first person, the way it's written. *With my present realisation, can I master the Light-of-Death when the time comes?* It isn't morbid and it isn't rhetorical. It wants an honest estimate, informed by what actually happened last night rather than by what you hope. If your awareness collapses every single time you fall asleep, you have your answer, and the answer is allowed to be no.

And a caution about the eight hours. If you stop remembering dreams entirely, don't take that as progress by default. The tradition's own line is that this reading goes two ways, and the thing that tells them apart isn't the nights — it's the days.

## Analytical Case Study: The Man Who Stopped Dreaming

The claim is specific and it's about a structural change, not a mood.

> Buddha taught that an individual who has broken through the conception skandha will in their sleeping state have the same degree of awareness as during wakefulness. Some cultivation schools describe this by saying the individual doesn't dream anymore, which simply means that the resulting stage of awareness during dreams has the same clarity as during wakeful states… Since the dream state and wakeful awareness are the same, we say this is a state of "no dreaming."[^4]

The conception skandha is the part of a person that does the labelling, and breaking through it is glossed here as having purified the sixth consciousness — the sorting, naming mind.[^4] So *no dreaming* doesn't mean the nights went blank. It means the difference between night and day stopped being a difference, and the tradition ran out of a word for that and used the nearest one.

Then, three sentences later, the same passage hands you the confound:

> In Taoism, Chuang Tzu said that there are two types of people who don't dream: the enlightened (those with Tao) and the very stupid.[^4]

Picture two men reporting the same thing. Neither dreams. Neither has dreamt in years. Ask them both and you get the same sentence, in the same untroubled tone, and there's nothing in either report to separate them — because the marker is an absence, and an absence made by clarity and an absence made by having very little going on look exactly alike from outside and from inside.

That's the shape almost every marker in this material has, and here, unusually, the source says so itself. What it says next is the interesting part. The Chuang Tzu line gets offered as evidence that the schools agree: *once again we find that an independent matching of the principles of cultivation throughout the various schools.*[^4] But the thing the schools have matched on is a limit, not a finding. Chuang Tzu isn't confirming that no-dreaming indicates attainment. He's saying it indicates one of two opposite things.

Which leaves the practitioner with a usable rule anyway, and it's the same rule that separates fullness from depletion everywhere else in this material. The absence itself carries no information. What carries it is the waking hours on either side — whether the days have become clearer or simply quieter — and that's a reading somebody else can take about you, which is more than most of these markers allow.

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

The design of the test is its own strongest argument.[^1] A nightly, free, low-stakes transition standing in for one that happens once is sound reasoning about how to assess a capacity you can't otherwise reach, and it holds whatever you make of the rest. The breath instruction is unusually strong too, because it names a marker that arrives the same night.[^3]

🚩 SECONDARY WITHOUT PRIMARY throughout. The readiness question and the light classification come as the book quoting Garma C. C. Chang, *Teachings of Tibetan Yoga*, pp 99–101; the four dissolutions as the book quoting Erik Pema Kunsang's *Advice from the Lotus Born*, pp 80–81; the Kashmir Shaivite line via John Hughes, *Self Realization in Kashmir Shaivism*, p 45. ⚠ The join between the two — that sleep runs a shortened version of the death sequence — is doing the load-bearing work here and is stated in neither quotation. It's an inference from their adjacency.[^1][^2]

The transfer claim is the whole value of the diagnostic and it's uncheckable by construction: nothing that can be observed in sleep can be scored against an event nobody reports back from.[^1] No mechanism beyond the structural similarity is offered, and no case is cited.

Two more flags. 🚩 The dream classification on p 443 carries three excluded categories in its later rows, along with claims about psychics' intelligence and eye-sheen and about virgin children, sourced to Art Bell and Brad Steiger's *The Source* — recorded on the companion page, `[DO NOT FILE]`, and nothing here rests on them.[^4] And the standing scope limit applies: the Four Voids and the clear light of sleep sit on a ladder that footnote 518 calls false stages, with three real jobs — rest stops, verifications, motivational assists.[^5] This is the cleanest instance in the corpus of the second job being done as advertised.

Two tensions stay open. The passage teaches three stages and then says this school never really reaches the third,[^3] without saying what does. And the Chuang Tzu line limits the no-dreaming marker while being presented as corroborating it.[^4] Everything here is `[POPULAR SOURCE]`.

Open questions. Is there anything short of death — anaesthesia, syncope, the near-death reports — that could partially calibrate the transfer, and did any tradition try? And if the light exists whether it's noticed or not, is what's being trained the noticing, or only the conditions under which noticing becomes possible?

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Two attitudes to this practice sit within a few pages of each other, and following either would give you a very different few years. Take the first and you'd treat it as almost free. One breath before sleep, a marker the same night, no chakra to find, and a test that costs nothing and can't be faked to yourself because nobody's watching. On that reading dream yoga is the most accessible thing in the book, and the elaborate Tibetan version is overhead you can drop.

Take the second and you'd approach it the way you'd approach a controlled substance. The faculty being trained is the same one that operates in insanity and incoherence; going the wrong way can send you mad; the gut has to be sound first; and anyone already inclined to drift is told the practice will worsen exactly what's wrong with them.[^3] On that reading almost nobody who wants this should be doing it.

Both are stated, a paragraph apart, and neither is withdrawn. Read alongside [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/who-should-not-practice-dream-yoga|Who Should Not Practice Dream Yoga]], the split turns out to run between two different activities that share a name — cultivating the du-yin, which carries the hazard, and simply watching what already happens every night, which carries none.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

Behavioral mechanics — [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/white-night-the-rehearsal-of-death|The Night They Practiced Dying]]. Jones ran White Nights over and over across the last years of the Peoples Temple: loudspeakers at midnight, an announced emergency, the vat brought out, a thousand people drinking what they were told was poison and then standing in the dark waiting to die. And then nothing, and back to the bunks. That page's finding is that the drill was never the point. Each repetition made the act a little more ordinary, so that when the real night came, the behaviour was already worn in.

Put that next to the Four Voids of Sleep and the structure is identical — rehearsing the one event that can't be rehearsed — with the function turned inside out. The sleep test asks a question: *with my present realisation, can I master the Light-of-Death when the time comes?* The answer is allowed to be no, and a no is the useful result. The White Night asks nothing. The answer was arranged before the loudspeakers came on, and a no wasn't among the options.

What separates them isn't sincerity, and it isn't the content of the drill. It's where the result goes. In the sleep test the practitioner is the only one who learns anything; the failure is private, costs nothing, and changes what they do tomorrow. In the White Night the leader is the only one who learns anything — he's reading compliance off the room — and the participant's failure is visible, punishable, and never handed back to them as information.

Which gives a single question you can put to any rehearsal, religious or corporate or military: after the drill, who's holding the result? A rehearsal that returns its finding to the person rehearsing is building a capacity. A rehearsal that returns its finding to whoever ordered it is building compliance. And from inside, on the night, both of them feel like getting ready.

*One handshake is the section here. A second would restate the same boundary from a neighbouring page rather than open new ground.*

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** The one thing you actually need to be able to do happens once, can't be practised, and can't be reported on — so the tradition swapped in the boundary you cross twice a day and rested the whole practice on the claim that they're the same crossing. That claim can never be checked. What can be checked is tonight: one held breath, a marker within eight hours, and an honest answer to whether anyone was home when you went under. The test is well built and permanently uncalibrated, and that's probably the best anybody can do with this particular question.

**The edge left open.** Three stages are taught and the third is declared out of reach by this route, with nothing named that does reach it. And the marker for arrival — no more dreaming — is an absence that reads identically from the top of the ladder and the bottom, which the passage says out loud and then treats as agreement between schools.

**Generative questions:**

- The transfer from sleep to death can't be checked. Anaesthesia can. Next time you go under for something minor, notice what the last moment was like — and whether you notice anything at all is itself the reading.
- If you stop remembering dreams, the tradition says that means one of two opposite things. Ask somebody who's known you five years whether your days have got clearer or just quieter, and take their answer over your own.
- The people most drawn to this practice — the dreamy, the absent, the ones who already live half inside their own heads — are the ones told it will make them worse. How much of what you want from a practice is the thing it's for, and how much is more of what you already do too much of?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/who-should-not-practice-dream-yoga|Who Should Not Practice Dream Yoga]] — the hazards of cultivating the du-yin, against the costless observing of it
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/du-yin-and-the-psi-programmes|Du-Yin and the Psi Programmes]] — the consciousness this whole practice runs on, and where else it operates
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-three-fullness-signs|The Three Fullness Signs]] — absence-shaped markers with the same two-way confound
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/hsi-and-the-cessation-of-breath|Hsi and the Cessation of Breath]] — the other boundary approached by not interfering with it; between two breaths there, between waking and sleeping here
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-unproduced-is-the-test|The Unproduced Is the Test]] — the criterion the Light-of-Origin passage passes cleanly
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-meditation-belt|The Meditation Belt]] — the same reflex of reaching for the mundane cause first
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/false-stages-and-the-footnote-that-says-so|False Stages, and the Footnote That Says So]] — verification done as advertised, with nothing more claimed
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/white-night-the-rehearsal-of-death|The Night They Practiced Dying]] — the same rehearsal structure with the finding flowing the other way

# Icons of Essence: What a Tantric Image Actually Is

## Not an Idol, Not a Portrait — a Tuning Fork

When most Westerners see a many-armed deity painted in fierce color, they reach for one of two boxes: either it's an idol (something the worshipper confuses with God) or it's decorative religious art. Tantra uses a third box, and it's the interesting one. The image is a *tuning fork*. Strike it and it gives off a particular note. The deity has a "vibration" — an energy-signature, a flavor of divine Consciousness — and the painted form is built to make that note ring in you.[^1]

So the image isn't God, and it isn't a picture of God. It's a device pointing at an essence, calibrated to transmit a frequency. Wallis's phrase for this is exact: these are "icons of essence."[^2] You don't worship the fork. You let it tune you.

## The Feed: Why the Tradition Needs Images at All

The deeper you go into nondual Tantra, the more abstract the absolute gets — formless, beyond reckoning, impossible to indicate. That's a problem for a practitioner with a human nervous system. You can't meditate on "impossible to indicate." You need a handle. The image is the handle: a concrete form that compresses an otherwise unholdable energy into something a body can sit in front of and feel.

The key move is that the form is *expressive*, not *representational*. A portrait tries to look like its subject. An icon of essence isn't trying to look like anything — there is nothing it could resemble. It's trying to *do* something: to carry the energy-signature across to the viewer. That's why the artist's job is fidelity to the source's described energy, not anatomical realism.[^3]

## The Calibration (How the Form Carries the Note)

Every feature is a frequency-component. White body, three eyes, ten arms, a garland of skulls, a posture of repose or of fury — none of it is arbitrary, and none of it is portraiture. Each element is tuned to transmit some aspect of the deity's essence. Fierce deities aren't ugly or evil; their fierceness is a specific note — the raw, vivid, slightly terrifying beauty of embodied existence struck hard. (And fierce deities, Wallis notes, are an exclusive feature of nondual Tantra; the dualists barely use them.)

The safeguard built into the doctrine: **the symbol is never confused with the essence itself.**[^2] This is the precise inversion of "idolatry." The idolater forgets the image points beyond itself. The Tantric practitioner never forgets — the whole technology depends on remembering that the fork is a fork, that the note is what matters, and that the note lives in Consciousness, not in the paint.

## Implementation: How to Actually Use One

Sit in front of the form. Don't analyze it as a picture — that keeps you outside it, cataloguing limbs. Instead, treat each feature as a question: *what energy is this trying to make me feel?* The white body says luminous clarity; the three eyes say the powers of willing, knowing, acting; the weapons say the way that energy cuts. You're not decoding a code. You're letting the form ring its note until you find the same note already sounding in your own awareness.

The shift you're after: the moment the image stops being "out there" — a thing you're looking at — and becomes a map of something already in you. The deity's features get read internally, as your own capacities. That's the point of contact between this page and the entire nondual method: the icon is the on-ramp to recognizing that its essence is your essence.

## Analytical Case Study: The Trident as the Maximal Icon

The clearest demonstration of an icon of essence is the Trika's trident-maṇḍala. It's the doctrine pushed to its limit: an image so completely "of essence" that it stops being a picture of a deity at all and becomes a map of all reality, drawn on the practitioner's own body.

Three goddesses — Parā, Parāparā, Aparā — sit on lotus-thrones on the tips of a trident whose staff is visualized as coextensive with the meditator's spine. Every feature is a frequency-component of the cosmos: the swelling at the base is the five elements, the staff is the tattvas up to Māyā, the banner-knot at the palate is Māyā-tattva, the plinth at the third eye is Śuddhavidyā, the lotus above it is Īśvara, and Sadāśiva lies in śavāsana gazing up toward the higher light. All thirty-six tattvas are packed into the form. The trident itself emerges from the fontanelle and expresses Śiva-Śakti in three ascending powers — the All-pervasive, the Equalizing, the Transmental — and above the last, the three white lotuses sit "outside" time and space entirely.

This is the icon-of-essence claim with nothing held back. You aren't looking at a representation; you're being handed a device that, contemplated correctly, dissolves the boundary between the depicted reality and your own body. The fork and the listener become one instrument. And the secret at its center — the invisible Fourth, the Heart that reabsorbs the distinction between the worshipped and the worshipper — is precisely the note the whole elaborate image exists to make ring. The most complex icon in the tradition is built to deliver the simplest recognition: that the essence it points to is the one looking.

## Information Emission (What This Page Feeds the Vault)

This page gives the rest of the vault a way to read every visualized form without falling into either the idolatry-trap or the decoration-trap. Whenever a concept page describes a deity to be "visualized as white, four-armed, holding X and Y," this page supplies the operating instruction: those features are frequency-components, not portraiture, and they are meant to be read internally as the viewer's own capacities. It is the interpretive substrate under [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/trishula-mandala-trident-of-the-trika|the trident maṇḍala]], under the deity-descriptions of all [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/nine-sampradayas-overview|nine sampradāyas]], and under the practice of [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/micro-macrocosmic-deity-visualization-method|micro-macrocosmic correlation]], where the deity's features get mapped one-by-one onto the practitioner. Without this page, those descriptions read as exotic iconography; with it, they read as tuning instructions.

## Evidence / Tensions / Open Questions

Wallis frames the icon-of-essence doctrine partly to manage a cross-cultural problem: the deity illustrations in his own book risk being read as idolatry by Judeo-Christian-Islamic eyes, so he has to install the right interpretive frame before the reader turns the page.[^1] The tension worth flagging: he also concedes the artist used "conventions of Western art that allow readers to more easily connect" — which means the very images teaching the icon-of-essence doctrine are themselves partly Westernized for accessibility.[^3] Open question: how much energy-signature survives translation into a foreign visual idiom?

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Only Wallis sources this page directly, so the productive tension is between his insider account and the vault's critical-historical material on Tantric imagery. Wallis reads the fierce icon as a tuning fork for a divine energy — the form is *for* transmission, and its meaning is interior. White, working historically on the same fierce goddesses, reads the imagery as the surviving trace of cremation-ground cults where the fierceness was literal — actual blood, actual skulls, actual danger. Hold both and you get a real divergence about what the image *records*: Wallis hears a note meant to be struck inward; White sees a photograph of an older, bloodier rite that later got read as metaphor. Both agree on one thing — the form is non-arbitrary and dense with meaning. The split is over whether that meaning was always interior or was driven inward later. What that reveals: the same painting is either a meditation aid or a fossil, depending on which warrant you read it under — and the tradition itself performs exactly this conversion, turning the fossil into the fork.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

The bridge here is simple to state: an icon of essence is a compression device — it packs a large, hard-to-hold quality into a small form that triggers it on sight. That's a problem other domains solve too.

- **Behavioral-mechanics**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/anchoring-and-priming|Anchoring and Priming]] — a logo, a jingle, a brand mark works on the identical principle: a compact sensory form engineered to fire a whole bundle of associations instantly, without analysis. The structural parallel is exact — both the icon and the brand mark are "essence compressed into a trigger." Where they split is the direction of the arrow. The brand mark fires an association *outward* (buy this, feel that, about a product). The icon fires it *inward* (recognize this as your own nature). Reading them together exposes something neither field says alone: the same compression technology can be used to install a desire or to dissolve one, and the only difference is whether the trigger points at an object or at the viewer's own awareness.
- **Psychology**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/active-imagination-jung|Active Imagination]] (Jung) — Jung's symbolic image is also a charged form that carries more than it depicts, meant to be entered rather than decoded, and meant ultimately to be recognized as a content of one's own psyche. The Tantric icon and the Jungian symbol converge on "the image is a doorway, not a destination." The tension: Jung treats the image as arising *from* the unconscious (it comes up out of you), while the Tantric icon is handed *down* from a tradition (it's installed in you, by a master, to overwrite the persona with the divine). The insight the pair yields: an image-doorway can be either discovered or transmitted, and a whole spiritual technology hinges on which — self-generated symbol versus lineage-given icon are two different relationships to the same psychic mechanism. And it cuts both ways as a caution: a self-generated image can flatter the ego it arose from, while a transmitted icon can install a form the practitioner never tests against their own depths. Jung trusts what rises; Tantra trusts what is handed down by a master who already crossed. Neither is automatically safer — each guards against the other's characteristic failure.

- **History**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/relics-symbols-and-political-legitimacy|Relics, Symbols, and Political Legitimacy]] — a crown, a flag, a relic operates on the icon-of-essence logic: a physical object engineered to carry an intangible essence (sovereignty, nationhood, sanctity) that it points to but is never identical with. The structural match is the "compressed essence in a form that transmits it" move. The split is the direction and the danger: the political symbol is meant to bind allegiance *outward* to an institution, and its characteristic failure is idolatry of the state — the flag mistaken for the nation. The Tantric icon points *inward* and builds in the explicit safeguard that the symbol is never the essence. Holding the two together surfaces this: every powerful symbol risks being mistaken for the thing it points at, and Tantra's contribution is a built-in anti-idolatry clause that political symbolism almost never includes — which is exactly why crowns get worshipped and flags get died for, while the icon is meant to dissolve.

## The Live Edge

**The Sharpest Implication**
If the image is a tuning fork and the note lives in you, then the entire visible apparatus of religion — the statues, the paintings, the gilded forms — is scaffolding for a recognition that finally needs none of it. The icon's success is its own obsolescence: it works when it dissolves into the essence it pointed at, and a practitioner who still needs the picture hasn't finished hearing the note. That's an uncomfortable thing to do with a wall of beautiful art — to treat it as a ladder you're meant to climb off of.

**Generative Questions**
- If the icon must use Western artistic conventions to "connect" with modern viewers, has the energy-signature been re-tuned to a different note — and would a traditional practitioner even recognize the deity?
- Where exactly is the line between an icon of essence (points beyond itself) and an idol (confused with the essence) — is it a property of the image, or only of the viewer's attention?
- Could the brand-mark and the deity-icon be placed on one continuum of "compression triggers," and if so, what would a deliberately *liberating* logo look like?

## Connected Concepts
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/nine-sampradayas-overview|The Nine Sampradāyas]] — each sect is identified by its deity-form, mantra, and scripture; the icon is the visual half of that identity.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/trishula-mandala-trident-of-the-trika|The Trident Maṇḍala of the Trika]] — the most elaborate icon of essence in the system, mapping all 36 tattvas onto a visualized form along the spine.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/prakasha-and-vimarsha|Prakāśa and Vimarśa]] — the icon works because Consciousness is self-reflective; the image is a reflection the viewer recognizes as self.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/thirty-six-tattvas-overview|The Thirty-Six Tattvas]] — the metaphysical map an icon like the trident makes visible and enterable.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/tantric-theodicy-no-evil-only-ignorance|Tantric Theodicy]] — why a fierce, "horrific" form can be beautiful: nothing in existence is outside the divine to be excluded.

## Footnotes
[^1]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/wallis-tantra-illuminated|Wallis, Tantra Illuminated]] — l.1271–1276 (role of images; Judeo-Christian-Islamic discomfort; vibration / energy-signature / flavor of Consciousness). Scholar-practitioner; insider-systematic warrant.
[^2]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/wallis-tantra-illuminated|Wallis, Tantra Illuminated]] — l.1276 (direct: "icons of essence"; symbols point toward essence, never confused with the essence itself).
[^3]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/wallis-tantra-illuminated|Wallis, Tantra Illuminated]] — l.1276 (artist's fidelity to original sources plus Western conventions for reader connection).

# The Legacy of the Waves

## The Wind Stops and the Water Keeps Moving

Stand on a shore the morning after a storm. The wind has gone. The sky is clear, there is nothing pushing on the water any more, and the sea is still heaving. Nothing is causing that motion now. It is left over.

That is the whole image, and Bodri uses it twice, three hundred pages apart, in almost the same words.

> These stubborn stains on the original nature are like ocean waves that have been whipped up by the wind. **Even though the wind may suddenly cease, the turbulence of the waves will only gradually subside, and only if you refrain from providing them with any further energy.**[^1]

> **While the wind on the ocean may suddenly cease creating waves, the legacy of these waves will always take a while to subside** and disappear completely, and so it's this inherent habit energy that you focus working to transform at this stage of cultivation.[^2]

The word he lands on in the second version is *legacy*. Not residue, not remnant. A legacy is something you inherit and go on paying out.

## What the Wind Was, and What Stopping It Buys

The wind is the mechanism that generated the habits. On the scheme this book runs, that is the sixth consciousness discriminating and the seventh consciousness attaching liking and disliking to what it discriminates — the machinery that lays down habitual grooves as an ordinary by-product of functioning.

Awakening stops the wind. Bodri is precise about what that does and does not accomplish:

> Even after you see the Tao, **these residual habits of obscuration will still initially remain because you cannot sever them completely with one stroke.** While thoughts may arise and you're able to detach from them so that they don't affect you, upon enlightenment **you will still have the task of purifying the seeds of these thoughts at their source within the ālaya.**[^2]

Two separate things, and the distinction is the practically useful part of the page. **You can be detached from a thought and still be carrying the seed that produces it.** The detachment is real — the thought arises and does not move you. The seed is also real, and it is still in the storehouse, and it will keep producing.

So what awakening buys is not the absence of the waves. It is the end of the wind, plus the capacity to stand there without being knocked over.

## The Clause Everyone Skips

The first version of the image carries a conditional that the second version drops, and it does more work than the metaphor:

> …the turbulence of the waves will only gradually subside, **and only if you refrain from providing them with any further energy.**[^1]

That is not decoration. It converts the image from a description into an instruction, and the instruction is entirely negative. There is nothing to *do* about the waves. There is only something to stop doing.

Which explains why Bodri insists this stage has no fixed method:

> As Zen master Kuei-shan said in regards to this stage of attainment, **there is no fixed method or technique which you need to use**, but rather, you must practice according to your own situation and according to your own wisdom.[^2]

A stage whose whole content is *withhold energy* cannot have a curriculum, because a curriculum would be a set of things to do, and doing things is how energy gets supplied. This is the structural reason the post-awakening literature is so thin, and it is a better reason than the usual one about ineffability.

## What Actually Runs Down

Bodri names the specific contents, and the list is unglamorous:

> In this Stage of True Cultivation Practice, **the habitual energy streams of desire, anger, delusion, attachment, greed, pride** and other negative habits are the major targets of purification or elimination. They're like stubborn stains that pollute any realization of your inherently pure essence, and **because they still linger to some extent after enlightenment**, they're like polluted stains that must be eliminated.[^1]

And then the concession that gives the page its teeth:

> While they're not actually real from the ultimate or ontological sense, **you must still learn how to purify them away** so that they don't ever arise in the first place.[^1]

Unreal, and still requiring years of work. That is the position, stated without embarrassment. The waves are not made of anything; the water is not doing anything a wave-free sea isn't doing; and you still cannot get on with your life until they flatten.

He is also specific that discipline will not do it, and the example he picks is deliberately mundane:

> On the road of spiritual practice **you'll need the full flowering of prajñā wisdom to cut off the most subtle and hidden of idle thoughts because meditation without prajñā won't do this. Discipline won't do it either.** As a simple example, **you can refrain from sexual activities, but that doesn't cut off sexual desires.** Sexual desire, in fact, is relatively easy to abandon **as compared to lingering ego habits.**[^3]

Abstinence stops the behaviour and leaves the seed intact — which is the same two-layer point, run on the easiest possible case so that the hard one becomes visible. And note the ranking in the last sentence. Sexual desire is the *easy* one.

## The Flattening Is the Destination, Not the Cleanup

It would be easy to read all of this as housekeeping — the real event happened, and now there is tidying. Bodri blocks that reading directly, and the block is the most surprising sentence in the chapter:

> Imagine the immensity of this: **the task of purifying your thoughts and behavior, after all these samādhi achievements and realms of cultivation experience, is in essence the very path to enlightenment!** The path to enlightenment involves perfecting your mind and behavior, only now when you reach this stage you finally have the ability to really accomplish this task.[^6]

Read that against what came before it. Years of preparation, the samādhis, the dhyānas, the threshold event — and the thing all of it was *for* is behaving well, which is the item every beginner was told to work on in week one.

The sentence does not change; the meaning does. He says so explicitly a page later: *the sentence doesn't change at all, but the meaning is entirely different* — *do good and refrain from evil* means the Stage of Merit Accumulation when a beginner says it, and the Stage of True Cultivation Practice when someone on the far side of the threshold does.[^6]

And what the flattening looks like from outside is nothing at all:

> A Zen saying therefore encapsulates this by describing the character of someone after they've awakened in self-realization: **"He is not different from the person he was in former times, he only differs from his past conduct."**[^6]

> **"Before enlightenment — chop wood and carry water. After enlightenment — chop wood and carry water."**[^6]

Same water, same wood, same man. What has changed, Bodri says, is *the skillfulness of one's action as well as the motivation behind your deeds* — self-interest replaced by compassion or simply by *the need to serve the requirements of the task at hand.*[^6]

Which is the strongest argument on the page for why the waves matter. They are not noise obscuring an attainment that is otherwise complete. **The state of the water is the entire observable content of the attainment**, because there is nothing else about an enlightened person that shows.

## Implementation Workflow

Two years after something real happened, you catch yourself being sharp with the same person about the same thing you were always sharp about. The immediate reading is that nothing changed. Look more closely at the sequence: the irritation arose, you were sharp, and — this is the part to check — were you *carried*, or did you watch it happen and go along anyway? On this scheme those are different positions, and only the second is available post-threshold. The wave is unchanged. Your relationship to being in the water isn't.

Now the operative instruction, which is a subtraction. You notice the irritation and you decide to work on it — you examine where it came from, rehearse the conversation, resolve to handle it better. Every one of those is attention, and attention is what the conditional forbids: *only if you refrain from providing them with any further energy.* The counter-intuitive move is to do none of it. Not suppression, which is another operation — just the withdrawal of interest, repeated for as long as it takes, with no expectation of a result you can date.

And the honest calibration. Ch'ang Ch'ing wore out seven cushions after his enlightenment; the figures Bodri quotes are nine to ten years minimum, thirty for some.[^4] If you are three months in and the waves are still running, that is not a diagnosis. Nothing in this account predicts a fast decay, and the only thing that reliably lengthens it is checking.

## Analytical Case Study: Why the Same Image Arrives Twice, Three Hundred Pages Apart

It is worth taking the repetition seriously rather than treating it as authorial habit, because the two placements do different jobs and the difference tells you what the image is for.

**First placement, p 248.** It appears inside the discussion of purifying the *volition skandha* — the layer of subtle motivational impulses and deep conditioning — and it arrives immediately after the claim that *it's only after you have seen the Tao and awakened to your true nature… that you can finally gradually begin to accomplish this task.*[^1] Here the image is doing **licensing** work: it explains why the task *starts* at awakening rather than finishing there.

**Second placement, p 574.** It appears inside the Tantric concordance, mapping the Stage of Learner's Union onto the volition and consciousness skandhas and onto Taoism's *breaking emptiness for the return to the Tao*.[^2] Here the image is doing **translation** work: whatever vocabulary a tradition uses for the post-awakening stretch, the same wave-decay is what it is describing.

Same picture, two functions — and the second is the one that matters for the book's project, because it is offered as the invariant that survives when the terminology is stripped off. Every tradition Bodri lists at that point ends up with a phase after the threshold in which something left over runs down.

There is one more thing the doubling reveals, and Bodri does not comment on it. **The conditional clause survives only in the first version.** The p 574 restatement says the legacy *will always take a while to subside* and drops *only if you refrain from providing them with any further energy*. The instruction is present when the image is licensing a practice and absent when it is doing comparative work — which is the exact place a reader looking for cross-tradition invariants would go, and the exact place they would come away with a picture of automatic decay.

## The Two Places the Metaphor Breaks

Worth naming, because the image is persuasive enough to do damage.

**Waves have no seeds.** Ocean turbulence decays through friction and nothing regenerates it. But the doctrine Bodri is illustrating says the habits *are* regenerated, from seeds in the ālaya, which is why he pivots from the metaphor straight to *purifying the seeds of these thoughts at their source*.[^2] A wave has no source once the wind stops; a habit does. The image understates the problem, and it understates it in the reassuring direction.

**Waves decay on their own; habits require a specific withholding.** The metaphor's whole affective payload is that time does the work. The conditional says otherwise. Read the image without the clause — which is how it reads at p 574 — and you get patience where the doctrine asks for vigilance.

Both breaks fail the same way. **The picture is gentler than the claim**, which makes it exactly the kind of metaphor that survives transmission and arrives with its instruction missing.

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

**Strongest support.** The abstinence example is the strongest thing on the page precisely because it is trivial.[^3] Refraining from an act plainly does not remove the desire for it — everyone has checked this personally — and the two-layer structure follows immediately without any doctrinal commitment. The rest of the argument is that observation generalised.

**The tension the source does not close.** The habits are *not actually real from the ultimate or ontological sense* and *you must still learn how to purify them away*.[^1] Bodri states both in one sentence and offers no account of what purifying an unreal thing consists of, or why an unreal thing takes decades to purify.

**A second tension, on the conditional.** The instruction to withhold energy appears in the p 248 version and is absent from the p 574 restatement.[^1] [^2] The version that circulates as the cross-tradition invariant is the one without the instruction.

**A third, on the metaphor's fit.** Wave decay is unforced and source-free; the doctrine's habits are seed-driven and require active withholding. The metaphor contradicts the mechanism it illustrates on both counts, in the direction of reassurance.

**A fourth, on citation.** The Kuei-shan attribution at p 574 is given as a general report of what the master said *in regards to this stage*, without quotation or locator, immediately before a quotation of the same master that *is* given verbatim.[^2] The unquoted report is doing argumentative work the quoted line does not support. `[SINGLE SOURCE]`.

**And the standing scope limit.** The stage whose entire content is this wave-decay is a rung of an apparatus footnote 518 calls false stages, whose three real jobs it names as rest stops, verifications and motivational assists.[^5] For this page the bite is unusual: a stage with no method, no curriculum and no datable completion is barely a stage at all, which is nearer to the footnote's position than to the ladder's.

**Open questions.** If the seeds regenerate the habits, what makes the decay monotonic — why should the water flatten at all rather than reaching a steady state? And is there any account in the literature of a practitioner whose waves *didn't* subside, or does the doctrine's structure make that outcome unreportable, since a person still turbulent at year thirty is reclassified as never having crossed?

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Read with [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/three-ways-we-sabotage-ourselves|Three Ways We Sabotage Ourselves]], this page names what the wind was. That page's chain — discrimination accumulates, becomes habit, habit becomes karmic force — is the wave-generating mechanism, described from the other end. **Awakening removes the generator and leaves the inventory**, which is why the two pages have to be read together: one is about the machine, the other about the stock it produced before it was switched off.

Against [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/sudden-and-gradual-both-have-places|Sudden and Gradual Both Have Places]], this is the mechanism for that page's third phase. There the claim is that the post-awakening stretch is gradual and cannot be hurried; here is why — the decay rate is a property of the water, not of your effort, and the only variable you control is whether you add energy.

With [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/cause-side-and-effect-side|Cause Side and Effect Side]] the fit is exact and slightly awkward. The waves run in the habit energies, which are volition-skandha material and therefore causal-ground work — meaning the wave-decay stage sits *before* the effect-side transformations, not after. **The wave metaphor makes the remaining task sound like an epilogue; the cause-and-effect architecture says it is the middle of the book.**

Against [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-two-ways-to-stall|The Two Ways to Stall]], there is a real distinction to hold. That page's failures are things a practitioner *does* — clinging to the attainment, adopting a superior position. The waves are things that merely persist. Confusing the two produces the characteristic post-awakening error in both directions: treating residual habit as a moral failure, or treating a genuine stall as residue that will subside if ignored.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**Extinction does not erase; it overlays** — [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/endocannabinoids-fear-extinction-neural-plasticity|Endocannabinoids and Fear Extinction: Neural Plasticity Through the CB1 System]]. That page's finding is that extinction learning does not delete the original fear association. The infralimbic cortex builds a new inhibitory memory on top of an intact one, CB1 signalling gates the process, and the original association remains available — which is why extinguished fears return under stress, in a new context, or simply with time. The structural match with the wave legacy is close, and the disagreement between them is the productive part. Bodri's picture is **decay**: the turbulence runs down and eventually disappears completely. The neuroscience picture is **suppression by overlay**: nothing runs down, a competing trace is built alongside, and the outcome depends on which trace wins retrieval in a given moment. **What the pairing gives that neither gives alone is a test that distinguishes them, and it is the same test in both fields.** If the habit is decaying, it should weaken uniformly across contexts. If it is being overlaid, it should look extinguished in the practice context and return intact in a novel or stressful one. That is exactly the observation the cultivation literature keeps recording without a framework for it — the adept who is immovable in the hall and recognisable at the deathbed, T'ien-wang Wu lucid about the one who is not in pain and crying anyway. On the overlay reading that is not a partial attainment or a failure of the wave to subside. It is renewal, and it is what an intact trace does when the context changes hard enough. Which supplies a prediction Bodri's model cannot make and his own case material already satisfies: **the decay should look complete right up until the first genuinely novel stressor, and then not.**

*One handshake.* A second — that the instruction is to withhold rather than to act — is the standing-rule material already handshaken from this hub through the ironic-process pairing, and repeating it would be restatement.

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** **The image says the sea flattens by itself and the doctrine says it flattens only while you withhold energy — and because the version that travels between traditions is the one with the conditional stripped off, the comparative literature has inherited a picture of automatic recovery from a tradition that never claimed one.**

**Generative questions.**
- If the seeds regenerate the habits, what makes the decay monotonic rather than steady-state — and does the tradition have an answer, or does the metaphor simply cover the gap?
- On the overlay reading, an "extinguished" habit returns intact under a novel stressor. Is there anything in the cultivation literature that distinguishes renewal from retrogression, or are they the same event under two doctrinal descriptions?
- A stage with no method, no curriculum and no datable end is hard to distinguish from no stage. What work is the *naming* of this stage doing, if not method-work?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/three-ways-we-sabotage-ourselves|Three Ways We Sabotage Ourselves]] — the wind, described as machinery
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/sudden-and-gradual-both-have-places|Sudden and Gradual Both Have Places]] — the third phase this page supplies the mechanism for
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/cause-side-and-effect-side|Cause Side and Effect Side]] — which places the wave-decay in the middle of the path rather than at its end
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-two-ways-to-stall|The Two Ways to Stall]] — active failures, against which mere residue must be distinguished
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/discard-until-what-cannot-be-discarded-remains|Discard Until What Cannot Be Discarded Remains]] — the seven cushions, and the pace this stage actually runs at
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/false-stages-and-the-footnote-that-says-so|False Stages, and the Footnote That Says So]] — the conventional status of a stage with no method
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/endocannabinoids-fear-extinction-neural-plasticity|Endocannabinoids and Fear Extinction]] — overlay rather than decay, and the test that separates them

## Footnotes

[^1]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/bodri-various-stages-of-the-spiritual-experience|Bodri, The Various Stages of the Spiritual Experience]] — p 248. The first wave image, **with the conditional clause** — *only if you refrain from providing them with any further energy*; the volition-skandha framing; the list of habitual energy streams (desire, anger, delusion, attachment, greed, pride); *while they're not actually real from the ultimate or ontological sense, you must still learn how to purify them away*; *it's only after you have seen the Tao… that you can finally gradually begin to accomplish this task*. `[POPULAR SOURCE]`
[^2]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/bodri-various-stages-of-the-spiritual-experience|Bodri, The Various Stages of the Spiritual Experience]] — p 574. The second wave image — *the legacy of these waves* — **without the conditional clause**; the Learner's Union concordance with the volition and consciousness skandhas, Zen's mastering birth and death, and Taoism's *breaking emptiness for the return to the Tao*; *you cannot sever them completely with one stroke*; *purifying the seeds of these thoughts at their source within the ālaya*. The Kuei-shan claim that there is *no fixed method or technique* is reported without quotation or locator, immediately before a verbatim Kuei-shan quotation on a different point — `[SINGLE SOURCE]` on the reported claim. `[POPULAR SOURCE]`
[^3]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/bodri-various-stages-of-the-spiritual-experience|Bodri, The Various Stages of the Spiritual Experience]] — p 248. *Meditation without prajñā won't do this. Discipline won't do it either*; the abstinence example; sexual desire ranked as *relatively easy to abandon as compared to lingering ego habits*. The Vasubandhu line on the seventh consciousness's four passions on the same page is footnoted to **Francis Cook trans., *Three Texts on Consciousness Only*, Numata 1999, p 378**, and the Ramakrishna line to ***The Spiritual Teaching of Ramana Maharshi*, Shambhala 1988, p x** — a Ramakrishna quotation sourced to a Ramana volume. Instance of the standing compendium-citation habit; neither is used on this page. `[POPULAR SOURCE]`
[^4]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/bodri-various-stages-of-the-spiritual-experience|Bodri, The Various Stages of the Spiritual Experience]] — p 209, quoting Nan Huai-Chin via ***Grass Mountain*, p 99**. The nine-to-ten-years and thirty-years figures; Ch'ang Ch'ing and the seven cushions. Cite as Bodri citing the Grass Mountain transcript. `[POPULAR SOURCE]`
[^6]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/bodri-various-stages-of-the-spiritual-experience|Bodri, The Various Stages of the Spiritual Experience]] — pp 249–250. *The task of purifying your thoughts and behavior… is in essence the very path to enlightenment*; *the sentence doesn't change at all, but the meaning is entirely different*; *he is not different from the person he was in former times, he only differs from his past conduct*; the chop-wood-carry-water couplet; skillfulness and motivation as what changes. Both Zen sayings are given without attribution or locator. `[POPULAR SOURCE]`
[^5]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/bodri-various-stages-of-the-spiritual-experience|Bodri, The Various Stages of the Spiritual Experience]] — footnote 518, p 511. The conventional status of the stage this decay constitutes, and the three functions named for the apparatus. `[POPULAR SOURCE]`
